title: Janusz Korczak turned down a hiding place on the Aryan side and marched with some two hundred children to the train to Treblinka

trailer.text: Janusz Korczak, a Polish Jewish pediatrician, author and educator from Warsaw, directed the Dom Sierot orphanage, which he had designed himself for Jewish children.
In 1940 the Germans established the Warsaw ghetto, and the orphanage was forced to move into it. Korczak went with the children even though he had repeatedly been offered shelter on the “Aryan side”.
In the ghetto he went from door to door and collected food, warm clothes and medicines for the children.
In August 1942 he boarded the train to Treblinka with some two hundred children.
There they all died in the gas chambers, together with him, with Stefa and with the staff members.

stations.title: A Warsaw boy who became a pediatrician

paragraphs.text: Janusz Korczak is the pen name of Henryk Goldszmit.
According to Yad Vashem, he was born on 22 July 1878 in Warsaw, to an assimilated Jewish family.
His father was a prominent lawyer and the sole provider of the household. He died after an illness in 1896.
Korczak was an author, a pediatrician and a pedagogue.
He dedicated his life to caring for children, particularly orphans.
According to My Jewish Learning, he saw himself as both a Pole and a Jew, and was active in both communities.
According to a Yad Vashem press release, in 1909 Korczak met Stefania Wilczyńska, Stefa, and the two began working together.
In 1911–1912 he became the director of the Dom Sierot orphanage in Warsaw. He had designed this home himself for Jewish children.
A republic of children was established in the home, with its own small parliament, court and newspaper.
The children regularly convened a court to hear grievances and dispense justice.
According to Yad Vashem, during the first six months Korczak accused himself six times in the children's court, for different infractions.
His book “The Child’s Right to Respect” came out in 1929. According to a blog on the Times of Israel, it appeared at a time when corporal punishment was acceptable.
Holocaust survivor Yitzhak Belfer grew up in the orphanage. He said that he arrived there at the age of seven and was educated under Korczak for eight years.

stations.title: A voice on the radio and visits to Ein Harod

paragraphs.text: According to a blog on the Times of Israel, in 1933 the Polish government awarded him the Silver Cross of Polonia Restituta.
According to the National WWII Museum, in 1937 he received the “Golden Laurel” of the Polish Academy of Literature.
In the 1930s Korczak had a radio program, and it was heard throughout Poland.
The program was closed down because of growing antisemitism, and he lost his position as a radio host.
Korczak traveled to Palestine under the British Mandate. He stayed in Kibbutz Ein Harod and observed the kibbutz's educational system.
Stefa also visited Palestine three times, between 1931 and 1938, and stayed at Ein Harod.

stations.title: In the ghetto: door to door

paragraphs.text: At the end of November 1939, the German authorities required every Jew to wear a white armband with a blue Star of David. Korczak refused to wear it and refused to remove his Polish Army officer's uniform, even though he was imprisoned for some time.

According to the National WWII Museum, after the orphanage was moved to the Warsaw Ghetto, Korczak complained at Gestapo headquarters about a German soldier who had confiscated a cart of potatoes he had tried to bring into the ghetto. He was then arrested because he was not wearing the star, beaten, and thrown into a prison cell.
After the imprisonment a doctor found fluid in his lungs and told him this was a sign of heart failure.
When Korczak was released from prison a month later, the children of the orphanage asked him why he had shouted at the Germans, and whether he had been scared.
At the beginning of 1940 there were about 150 children in the orphanage.
In the autumn of 1940 the Germans established the Warsaw ghetto. Starvation and disease caused tens of thousands of deaths, and because of them many children were left orphaned and unattended.
The orphanage was forced to move into the ghetto. Korczak went with the children even though he had repeatedly been offered shelter on the “Aryan side”.
According to aboutholocaust.org, by the summer of 1942 the home had around 200 children.
He went from door to door and gathered food, warm clothes and medicines.
In his diary he tracked the children's weight loss. As a doctor, he understood that his own fatigue came from malnutrition, from less than 800 calories a day.
The home continued to operate according to its pre-war arrangements, and the children continued to take part in the administration and in the public trials.
On 15 July 1942 Korczak sent out invitations to a play at the orphanage.
The last play, Tagore's The Post Office, was staged in the orphanage by the theater class of 1942 during the big deportation in the ghetto.
According to the museum, the children performed it on 18 July 1942.
According to Yad Vashem, the people of Ein Harod arranged papers for Stefa to leave Poland. She refused, and moved with Korczak and the children into the ghetto.
At the end of July 1942 Polish friends offered to hide Korczak, or to obtain forged papers for him.
He and the staff decided not to save themselves, and to keep caring for the children.
On the morning of the deportation German police arrived and ordered the staff to evacuate the building.
According to the Jerusalem Post, Korczak dressed the children in their best clothes and stayed with them the entire time.
According to a blog on the Times of Israel, he told them they were going on a train to a pleasant rural place with plenty of fresh air.
The children marched in rows to the Umschlagplatz gathering point, with Korczak in the lead.
Stefa and the rest of the staff marched with them.
According to USHMM, witness accounts describe the march through the ghetto as orderly and dignified.
In a poem by the poet Władysław Szlengel, a man ran up to Korczak and told him that Herr Brandt had signed his release. According to the poem, Korczak kept marching with contempt.
According to the blog on the Times of Israel, a Nazi soldier recognized him and offered to save him by sending him to Theresienstadt, and he refused.
Korczak boarded the train to Treblinka with the children.
There they all died in the gas chambers, together with Stefa and with the staff members.
According to USHMM, they were almost certainly killed on the day they arrived.
Michał Wróblewski, a teacher whom Korczak had helped find work, said that the decision to go with the children to the train was part of his nature.
According to aboutholocaust.org, there is no way of knowing for sure why he chose to accompany the children. Even so, his writings always place the needs of the child first.
After the deportation a friend smuggled Korczak's diary out of the ghetto.
The diary, with notes, memories and observations, was published in Poland in 1958.
There are 17,000 stones in the symbolic cemetery at Treblinka. Only one of them bears the name of an individual, and the name is Korczak.
At Yad Vashem in Jerusalem stands a sculpture by Boris Saktsier that honors Korczak and his actions.
On 9 August 2015 Holocaust survivors and young people commemorated the educator and his children at the event “Kites for Korczak”.
Władysław Szpilman wrote in “The Pianist” that Korczak's true value was not in what he wrote but in the fact that he lived as he wrote.
According to USHMM, the Polish and Jewish communities salute him.
According to My Jewish Learning, some of the ultra-Orthodox in Warsaw's Jewish community claimed that the progressive orphanage was “too Polish”.
They claimed this even though the home kept kosher and observed the Sabbath and holidays.

disagreements.question: In what year was Korczak born?

versions.says: Yad Vashem: on 22 July 1878
aboutholocaust.org: in 1879
My Jewish Learning: in 1878 or 1879, because his father did not register his birth

disagreements.question: In what year did he become director of the orphanage?

versions.says: Yad Vashem (educational material): in 1911–1912
USHMM: in 1911
Yad Vashem (press release): in 1912

disagreements.question: How many times and when did he visit Palestine?

versions.says: Yad Vashem: in 1934 and in 1936
My Jewish Learning: twice in the 1930s
Blog on the Times of Israel: every year, from 1934 to 1936

disagreements.question: Did he want to immigrate to Palestine?

versions.says: Yad Vashem: he decided to immigrate, and in 1939 met with Yitzhak Gruenbaum of the Jewish Agency to consult about the immigration
Blog on the Times of Israel: in 1936 he was invited to move to Palestine, and refused because he did not want to abandon the children

disagreements.question: When were the deportation and the death at Treblinka?

versions.says: Yad Vashem: the deportation and the boarding of the train were on 5 August 1942
USHMM: the police arrived on the morning of 5 or 6 August 1942
The National WWII Museum: the Nazis came to the orphanage on 6 August 1942
Yad Vashem names database: the recorded date of death is 6 August 1942
Jerusalem Post: he was exterminated on 7 August 1942
Yad Vashem (2017): 8 August 2017 marked 75 years since the deportation

disagreements.question: How many children and how many staff members went with him?

versions.says: Yad Vashem: about 200 children, about 12 staff members, and Stefa
Yad Vashem (press release): 200 children
The National WWII Museum: nearly 200 orphans
My Jewish Learning: 192 orphans and ten staff members, including Korczak
Blog on the Times of Israel: 196 orphans

claims.quote: Witness accounts describe the group’s march through the ghetto as orderly and dignified.

claims.text: לפי שיר של המשורר ולדיסלב שלנגל שהמוזיאון מצטט, בזמן הצעדה רץ אליו אדם ואמר שהר ברנדט חתם על שחרורו, וקורצ'אק המשיך לצעוד בבוז.
claims.quote: Sir, Herr Brandt here has signed your release!

claims.text: לפי הבלוג ב-Times of Israel, חייל נאצי זיהה את קורצ'אק והציע להצילו בשליחתו לטרזינשטט, אך הוא סירב.
claims.quote: He approached Dr. Korczak and told him he could save him from Treblinka by sending him instead to the concentration camp of Theresienstadt

claims.text: לפי USHMM, הילדים ומטפליהם נהרגו כמעט בוודאות ביום שבו הגיעו לטרבלינקה.
claims.quote: The children and their caretakers were almost certainly all killed the day they arrived at Treblinka.

claims.text: לפי My Jewish Learning, מיכל ורובלבסקי, מורה שקורצ'אק עזר לו למצוא עבודה, אמר שההחלטה האחרונה ללכת עם הילדים לרכבת הייתה חלק מטבעו של קורצ'אק.
claims.quote: As for that last decision to go with the children to Treblinka, it was part of his nature. It was who he was.

claims.text: לפי aboutholocaust.org, אין דרך לדעת בוודאות מדוע בחר ללוות את הילדים, אך כתביו מציבים תמיד את צורכי הילד בראש.
claims.quote: We have no way of knowing for sure why he chose to do so, but his writings consistently place the need of the child as paramount.

claims.text: לפי המוזיאון, יומנו של קורצ'אק הוברח החוצה בידי חבר לאחר שגורש.
claims.quote: Korczak’s diary, which was smuggled out by a friend after he had been deported, included these among the last lines he ever wrote:

claims.text: לפי יד ושם, בגטו כתב קורצ'אק יומן עם רשימות, זיכרונות והתבוננויות; היומן פורסם בפולין ב-1958.
claims.quote: In the ghetto, Korczak wrote a diary with notes, memories and observations; in it he portrayed his inner world and personal view on life in the ghetto. This diary was published in Poland in 1958.

claims.text: לפי מוזיאון מלחמת העולם השנייה, מבין 17,000 האבנים בבית הקברות הסמלי באתר הזיכרון בטרבלינקה רק אחת נושאת שם של אדם יחיד, ושם נרשם קורצ'אק.
claims.quote: Among the 17,000 stones standing as a symbolic cemetery at the Treblinka memorial, only one bears the name of an individual:

claims.text: לפי יד ושם, ב-9 באוגוסט 2015 נערך אירוע "עפיפונים לקורצ'אק" שבו ניצולי שואה ובני נוער הנציחו את המחנך ואת הילדים שבטיפולו.
claims.quote: Kites for Korczak: Holocaust Survivors and Youth Honor Memory of Educator and the Children in His Care

claims.text: המוזיאון מצטט את ולדיסלב שפילמן בספרו "הפסנתרן": ערכו האמיתי של קורצ'אק לא היה במה שכתב אלא בכך שחי כפי שכתב.
claims.quote: Korczak’s true value was not in what he wrote but in the fact that he lived as he wrote.

claims.text: לפי USHMM, קורצ'אק היה גאה במוצאו הפולני ובזהותו היהודית כאחד, והקהילות הפולנית והיהודית מצדיעות לו.
claims.quote: Korczak was equally proud of his Polish nationality and his Jewish identity.

claims.text: לפי My Jewish Learning, חלק מהאולטרא-אורתודוקסים בקהילה היהודית בוורשה טענו שבית היתומים המתקדם היה פולני מדי, אף שקיים כשרות ושבת וחגים.
claims.quote: Among the ultra-Orthodox, there were some who claimed that the progressive orphanage–though it observed the basic rules of traditional Judaism, by keeping kosher and celebrating the Sabbath and Jewish holidays–was too Polish.

claims.text: לפי aboutholocaust.org, קורצ'אק נולד בשם הנריק גולדשמיט ב-1879.
claims.quote: Born Henryk Goldszmit in 1879, the son of a prominent Warsaw lawyer

claims.text: לפי My Jewish Learning, קורצ'אק נולד בשם הנריק גולדשמיט למשפחה יהודית חילונית בוורשה ב-1878 או ב-1879, משום שאביו לא רשם את לידתו.
claims.quote: Januz Korczak was born Henryk Goldszmit to a secular Jewish family in Warsaw, in 1878 or 1879 (his father failed to register his birth, hence the uncertainty).

claims.text: לפי USHMM, ב-1911 קורצ'אק קיבל תפקיד בהנהלת בית יתומים יהודי חדש בוורשה.
claims.quote: In 1911, Korczak took a position leading a new Jewish orphanage in Warsaw.

claims.text: לפי יד ושם, ב-1912 נעשה קורצ'אק מנהל בית יתומים יהודי בוורשה.
claims.quote: In 1912, Korczak became the director of a Jewish orphanage in Warsaw.

claims.text: לפי My Jewish Learning, קורצ'אק ביקר בפלשתינה פעמיים בשנות ה-30.
claims.quote: He visited Palestine twice in the 1930s.

claims.text: לפי הבלוג ב-Times of Israel, בכל שנה בין 1934 ל-1936 נסע קורצ'אק לפלשתינה.
claims.quote: Each year from 1934-1936 he traveled to Palestine and was immensely impressed with the kibbutzim

claims.text: לפי יד ושם, כשהמצב בפולין החמיר קורצ'אק החליט לעלות לפלשתינה וב-1939 נפגש עם יצחק גרינבוים מהסוכנות היהודית להתייעץ על תוכניות ההגירה.
claims.quote: When the situation worsened in Poland, Korczak decided to immigrate to Palestine, and in 1939 met with Yitzhak Gruenbaum, a member of the Jewish Agency, to consult with him about plans for immigration.

claims.text: לפי הבלוג ב-Times of Israel, ב-1936 הוזמן קורצ'אק לעבור לפלשתינה, אך סירב כי לא רצה לנטוש את ילדי בית היתומים.
claims.quote: But Dr. Korczak refused the offer because he would not abandon the children in his orphanage.

claims.text: לפי יד ושם, ב-5 באוגוסט 1942, בגל גירושים בן חודשיים, אספו הנאצים את קורצ'אק, וילצ'ינסקה ו-200 ילדי בית היתומים.
claims.quote: On 5 August 1942, during a two-month wave of deportations from the ghetto, the Nazis rounded up Korczak, Wilczynska and the 200 children of the orphanage.

claims.text: לפי המוזיאון, ב-6 באוגוסט 1942 הגיעו הנאצים לבית היתומים כדי לגרש לטרבלינקה את קורצ'אק, עמיתיו וכמעט 200 יתומי דום סיירוט.
claims.quote: On August 6, 1942, the Nazis descended on Korczak’s orphanage to deport him, his co-workers, and the nearly 200 orphans of Dom Sierot to Treblinka.

claims.text: לפי מאגר השמות של יד ושם, קורצ'אק נרצח בשואה, ומקום המוות הרשום הוא טרבלינקה, פולין, בתאריך 06/08/1942.
claims.quote: Henryk Janusz was murdered in the Shoah. Place of death: Treblinka, Poland, 06/08/1942.

claims.text: לפי ג'רוזלם פוסט, קורצ'אק הושמד בטרבלינקה ב-7 באוגוסט 1942.
claims.quote: On August 7, 1942, Korczak was exterminated in the Treblinka death camp.

claims.text: לפי יד ושם (7.8.2017), ב-8 באוגוסט 2017 מלאו 75 שנים לגירוש קורצ'אק, סטפה וילדי בית היתומים מגטו ורשה לטרבלינקה.
claims.quote: Tomorrow, 8 August 2017, marks the 75th anniversary of the deportation of Janusz Korczak, Stefa Wilczynska and the children of their orphanage, from the Warsaw ghetto to Treblinka.

claims.text: לפי My Jewish Learning, 192 יתומים ועשרה אנשי צוות, כולל קורצ'אק, נהרגו עם הגעתם לטרבלינקה.
claims.quote: 192 orphans and ten staff members, including Korczak

claims.text: לפי הבלוג ב-Times of Israel, קורצ'אק היהודי, שנולד כהנריק גולדשמיט, סירב להצעה והגיע לטרבלינקה עם 196 יתומים, ספרים וצעצועים.
claims.quote: Dr. Janusz Korczak, the Jew born as Henryk Goldszmit, refused the offer and arrived at Teblinka with his 196 orphans, books and toys in hand.

claims.text: יד ושם (הודעה לעיתונות): ב-1909
claims.quote: In 1909, she met Korczak and the two began working together.
